summary:
Legal recognition in India is now restricted by category rather than by self-declaration. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, passed by Parliament in March 2026, amends the 2019 statute so that legal recognition is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch (26 March 2026) quotes rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describing the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes a large share of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. An estimated two million people in India are transgender.

The constitutional baseline remains comparatively protective on paper. The Supreme Court has held that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity falls within the Article 15 prohibition of discrimination by "sex," and the Allahabad High Court extended this in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. The Supreme Court decriminalised same-sex acts in 2018. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units (GOV.UK country policy note, December 2025).

Criminal-law protection weakened with the replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Reporting by Frontline (6 September 2024) documents that the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried, removing safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence; trans people interviewed said they fear a resulting rise in assaults.

Identity documents and security checkpoints are recurring friction points. In November 2024 CISF personnel stopped Sakshi Jain, an openly transgender law student, at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 even though she presented her PAN card for verification. A transwoman in Kolkata alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at a station under the pretext of "checking gender." In June 2024, transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam described degrading treatment in custody. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to undergo a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026. The GOV.UK policy note assesses police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited rather than systemic, and likelier in conservative rural areas.

Transition-related care has a national funding channel. The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in August 2024 coverage notwithstanding, in April 2024, to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. Bans on conversion therapy issued by the Madras High Court in 2021 and by the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine providers still operating.

Two recognition channels sit alongside the amended statute. Article 15 jurisprudence continues to apply regardless of whether a person holds formal trans identity documents. The University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging in higher education on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Major religious-nationalist organisations, including the Vishva Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal, have labelled same-sex marriage a "Western attack on Indian culture" and have occasionally targeted Pride events.
tangentialFactors:
Documented hostility toward gender-nonconforming people is concentrated in official checkpoints and in custody, not in the statute alone. The three 2024 incidents at Chennai airport, on the railways in Kolkata and in Railway Protection Force custody in Assam all involved state personnel using identity verification or detention as the setting for harassment or assault.

Public attitudes are split and shifting rather than uniformly hostile. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found 59% of respondents still calling homosexuality "morally unacceptable," while a 2023 Gallup poll showed 53% support for same-sex marriage, and a 2021 Ipsos survey of urban internet users found 17% identifying as non-heterosexual or non-cisgender. Demographic studies report a high prevalence of verbal abuse and physical violence against sexual minorities.

Figures on the size of the trans population do not reconcile: the 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender, against an estimate of about two million used in current reporting.

Judicial intervention has been a sustained feature of the regime. The Madras High Court judgment in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police (W.P.No.7284 of 2021, 7 June 2021, Justice N. Anand Venkatesh), brought by a same-sex couple harassed by police, issued sweeping guidelines covering protection of LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

Political visibility exists at national level. Shabnam Mausi became the first transgender elected official in 1998, and transgender mayors and judges have served in office. In March 2026 Menaka Guruswamy became India's first openly LGBTQ+ member of the national Parliament.
localsOnly:
Welfare delivery is largely state-level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pension schemes, and several other states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.

The Ayushman Bharat national health insurance scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors face coercive medicine. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered the Tamil Nadu government in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Conversion therapy is prohibited by the Madras High Court (2021) and by the National Medical Commission (2022), but clandestine networks continue to operate nationwide. The University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging aimed at students on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in higher education.

Acceptance varies sharply by setting and is notably higher among urban youth and students at elite institutions, where campus support groups operate. Organisations such as GayBombay, Good as You in Bangalore and Sappho for Equality in Kolkata run support networks, and Pride events have been held annually in dozens of cities since the first parade in Kolkata in 1999.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not establish whether the March 2026 amendment has been notified and is in force, what implementing rules govern the identification of qualifying socio-cultural groups, or how recognition decisions are made in practice. This is unresolved on the present sources.

How the amended recognition scheme affects entry decisions, visa applications and the treatment of foreign trans nationals is not sourced. No material in the inventory addresses the gender marker on Indian visas, on e-Gate or arrival documentation, or on border screening of visitors.

The interaction between the amended statutory test and the Article 15 jurisprudence is unresolved here: the sources record both regimes but do not state whether courts have applied the constitutional protection to persons excluded from statutory recognition.

Reports of conversion-therapy providers operating despite the bans are documented as a general finding; the scale and locations of these networks are not sourced.

No post-2011 census count of transgender people exists in the inventory, and the relationship between the census figure and the current two-million estimate is unexplained.
